title: 2014 St Catherines Legal Studies Trial
notes: No multiple-choice answer key was found in the paper. Questions 4–6 share one textual stimulus; no figures were needed.

groups.stimulus: Samuel runs an anti-government website which he is using to organise a violent protest at parliament house due to Australia’s involvement in an international conflict. Andrew is a regular reader of the website and attends the protest where he is arrested after smashing a window of the parliamentary building.

questions.stem: Which of the following human rights may be best described as a collective right

options.A: Freedom from arbitrary detention
options.B: The right to join a trade union
options.C: Environmental rights
options.D: Voting rights

options.A: A court order giving the police the power to arrest a person
options.B: A court order requiring a person to be detained until trial
options.C: A court order which allows the police to search property
options.D: A court order requiring a person to be extradited overseas

options.C: Terrorism

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Andrew’s degree of involvement in criminal behaviour?

options.A: Accessory before the fact
options.B: Accessory after the fact
options.C: Principal in the first degree
options.D: Principal in the second degree

questions.answerNote: School key says A, but Andrew personally smashes the window, which looks like principal in the first degree (C). Key kept as published; see THSC 'St Catherines 2014 w. sol' mapping grid.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors affecting criminal behaviour are most likely the cause of Samuel and Andrew’s actions?

options.A: Economic factors
options.B: Social factors
options.C: Self Interest
options.D: Political factors

questions.answerNote: School key says A (economic), but a protest against involvement in an international conflict looks political (D). Key kept as published; see THSC 'St Catherines 2014 w. sol' mapping grid.

questions.stem: On her 14th birthday, Sinclair takes her parents car on a joy ride after drinking at her party. She is stopped by police after they see her driving erratically and she is charged with a range of driving offences. How does the concept of doli incapax apply to Sinclair in relation to these offences?

options.A: She cannot be charged with any criminal offence due to doli incapax
options.B: The prosecution must rebut the presumption of doli incapax to gain a conviction
options.C: The concept of doli incapax does not apply but no conviction can be recorded
options.D: The defence must raise the defence of doli incapax to secure an acquittal

questions.stem: According to the separation of powers in the Constitution of the Commonwealth of Australia, who has the power to enforce the law?

options.A: The Executive
options.B: The Legislature
options.C: The Judiciary
options.D: The Governor General

questions.stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates the recognition and enforcement of human rights by the Australian legal system.

options.A: When a court orders the release from custody of a 15 year old person
options.B: When a court declares that protest action by animal rights activists is legal
options.C: When students are denied access to classes for two weeks because of vandalism
options.D: When Australian parliament passes a law that makes discrimination illegal

questions.answerNote: School key says B; D (parliament legislating against discrimination) looks the better fit for recognition and enforcement. Key kept as published; see THSC 'St Catherines 2014 w. sol' mapping grid.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the responsibility to protect in international law?

options.A: Each nation must protect its own citizen due to state sovereignty
options.B: The international community must protect individuals from human rights abuses
options.C: Domestic governments and the international community share the duty to protect and promote human rights
options.D: Individuals are responsible for protecting their own rights using domestic and international legal measures

questions.answerNote: St Catherines 2014 HSC Trial mapping grid (Correct Answer column), in the THSC 'St Catherines 2014 w. sol' PDF (https://www.thsconline.net/s/yr12/Legal%20Studies/trialpapers.html).

questions.stem: How does the defence of mental illness differ from the other criminal defences?

options.A: The onus of proof is reversed from the prosecution to the defence
options.B: It is the only complete defence which if successful results in acquittal
options.C: The defence can only be used in offences against the person
options.D: It relies on the actions of the victim at the time of the offence

questions.answerNote: School key says D, but A (onus of proof reversed to the defence) is the accepted distinguishing feature of mental illness. Key kept as published; see THSC 'St Catherines 2014 w. sol' mapping grid.
